# tsuzuri

A personal blog: a portrait and bio on the home page, and posts underneath.
Each post can carry more than one translation, and a reader is served
whichever translation best matches the locales their browser sends.

## Getting started

```bash
npm install
```

## Commands

| Command                | What it does                                              |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm run dev`           | Serves the site locally with hot reload.                   |
| `npm run build`         | Builds the production bundle.                              |
| `npm run start`         | Serves a build produced by `npm run build`.                |
| `npm run format`        | Rewrites the project in place to its house style.          |
| `npm run format:check`  | Reports formatting drift without rewriting anything.       |
| `npm run lint`          | Lints the whole project; also checks formatting.           |
| `npm run typecheck`     | Type-checks the project. The test runner compiles without checking types, so this is the only thing that does. |
| `npm test`              | Runs the unit test suite.                                  |
| `npm run test:e2e`      | Runs the end-to-end suite. Builds the app and serves it first, so it needs a browser — `npx playwright install chromium` once per machine. |

## Layout

- `app/(site)/` — the reader-facing route group: the home page, the post
  detail page, and the small data module they both read from.
- `shared/` — code shared by more than one part of the app, independent of any
  one route. `shared/resolve-translation.ts` is the locale-fallback logic a
  post detail page calls into; `shared/blog-post-slug.ts` is the slug shape
  every post's `slug` is validated against.
- `shared/*.spec.ts` — unit tests, colocated with the code they cover.
- `e2e/` — end-to-end specs, kept apart from the unit tests above because they
  exercise the whole running app rather than one module in isolation.
- `docs/` — operational notes that do not belong in code comments, such as
  [deployment](docs/deployment.md).
- `.github/workflows/` — the checks that run on every pull request.

## Contributing

Changes go through a pull request rather than landing straight on `main`.
Before writing code, sketch the plan and get it approved — this catches a
misunderstood requirement while it is still cheap to redirect, rather than
after the diff exists. A pull request is reviewed by someone other than the
person who wrote it, and merges only once that review is clean and the checks
above pass.

# Deployment

Operational notes for running this site outside a local checkout. `npm run
build` produces what is served and `npm run start` serves it; everything below
is what a real deployment target adds around that pair.

## Environments

| Environment | Trigger                     | Notes                            |
| ----------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Production  | Push to `main`              | Serves the default locale first. |
| Preview     | Pull request opened/updated | One preview per pull request.    |

## Locale fallback

A reader's accepted locales come from their browser's `Accept-Language`
header. `shared/resolve-translation.ts` is what turns that preference list
into the translation a post detail page renders — see its own documentation
for the exact resolution order. Deployment does not change that order; it only
changes which posts and translations the deployed build carries.

## Rolling back

Redeploy the previous commit's build. There is no database to migrate back —
the post catalog and everything else the app reads live in the build itself —
so a rollback here is just a redeploy.

# Deployment

Operational notes for running this site outside a local checkout. `npm run
build` produces what is served and `npm run start` serves it; everything below
is what a real deployment target adds around that pair.

## Environments

| Environment | Trigger                     | Notes                            |
| ----------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Production  | Push to `main`              | Serves the default locale first. |
| Preview     | Pull request opened/updated | One preview per pull request.    |

## Locale fallback

A reader's accepted locales come from their browser's `Accept-Language`
header. `shared/resolve-translation.ts` is what turns that preference list
into the translation a post detail page renders — see its own documentation
for the exact resolution order. Deployment does not change that order; it only
changes which posts and translations the deployed build carries.

## Rolling back

Redeploy the previous commit's build. There is no database to migrate back —
the post catalog and everything else the app reads live in the build itself —
so a rollback here is just a redeploy.

content.text:
## Proposal: reader corrections on a post

**What a reader sees:** a small "Spot a mistake?" form at the bottom of a post's rendered body (in `app/(site)/posts/[slug]/page.tsx`), with a plain-text field for the correction and an optional email field for follow-up. Submitting posts it to the server and shows a thank-you state; no page reload needed for that to feel good, but a plain HTML `<form>` POST works too if we want to avoid client JS entirely.

**What gets captured, per submission:**
- the post's `slug`
- the `locale` of the translation the reader was actually looking at (from `resolveTranslation`'s result) — otherwise we can't tell which language version had the typo
- the correction text, capped at some short length (e.g. 500 chars)
- an optional contact email, not required

**The open decision — where a submission goes:**

Right now this site has no backend and no database at all — `docs/deployment.md` is explicit that "there is no database to migrate back," everything the app reads is baked into the build, and a rollback is just a redeploy. A corrections feature is the first thing that needs to *write* somewhere at runtime, so this is the real design decision, not the form UI:

1. **Forward to email** (a transactional email API, e.g. Resend/Postmark) from a server action/route handler. No new persistent state, no admin UI to build — corrections just land in an inbox. Adds one third-party dependency and one secret (API key) to manage in deploy config. Recommended default for a low-volume personal blog.
2. **Create a GitHub issue** via the GitHub API, since post content already lives in this repo. Keeps corrections next to the content they're about, but means embedding a repo-scoped token server-side and mapping submissions to issue titles/labels.
3. **Add a real datastore** (hosted KV/DB) and a page to review submissions. Most flexible, but it's a bigger addition — it turns "rollback = redeploy" into something that needs its own thought, and needs a review UI that doesn't exist yet.

I'd default to (1) unless there's a reason to want corrections tracked as repo issues or reviewed in an admin UI — worth confirming before building, since it changes what secrets and docs updates the PR needs.

**Abuse handling:** the site has no auth, so the endpoint needs basic protection independent of which destination we pick — a honeypot field plus a coarse rate limit (e.g. per-IP) so this can't become an open mail/issue relay.

**Where the code lives:** per `AGENTS.md`'s organization rule, the form, its validation, and the submit handler are only used by the post detail page, so they'd colocate under `app/(site)/posts/[slug]/` rather than `shared/` — unless we later want corrections on some other route, at which point the shared bit would move up. Input validation would use `zod` (already a dependency).

**Testing:** a unit test for the validation schema (empty text, over-length text, malformed email), and an e2e test that fills the form on a post page and asserts the thank-you state, stubbing whatever the chosen destination is so the suite doesn't hit a real inbox/API.

**Docs to touch:** `docs/deployment.md`'s "no database to migrate back" line stops being true if we ever pick option 3, and either way it'll need a line about whatever new secret (email API key or GitHub token) a deploy has to carry.

Let me know which delivery destination you want (I'd go with email-forwarding as the default) and I'll turn this into an actual implementation plan for the PR.
